827.title: Bhishma's fall
827.hook: losing every day to their own grandsire, the Pandavas walk across the field at night to ask him how he can be killed
827.howItsDone: Retellings of the Mahabharata keep the night when the Pandavas visit Bhishma's tent and he tells them how he can be overcome.

segments.voice: Your line yesterday was to be killed by you would be an honor. Twice Krishna leapt from the chariot and ran at him, and twice Arjuna pulled him back. And the old man is still standing. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

Night, and the Pandava camp is quiet in the wrong way. Another day has gone to Bhishma. He is the commander of the other side, and he is also the elder these brothers grew up calling grandsire. Yudhishthira can't see a way through. Then he remembers the first morning, when he walked over to Bhishma unarmed. Bhishma told him then that he could not fight for the Pandavas but would still give them counsel, and that the question of how he could be beaten should be asked again another time. So the brothers set their weapons aside, and with Krishna they walk across the dark field to the enemy's tent. Today, the brothers ask it.
screen: `ANOTHER DAY LOST TO BHISHMA.` → `A PROMISE OF COUNSEL.` → `ACROSS THE FIELD AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bhishma doesn't reach for a sword. In Ganguli's English, he welcomes them, asks why they've come, and offers to do whatever he can for them. Yudhishthira asks the question out loud. How can you be defeated? How can we win, when you stand in the way? It's an unbearable thing to ask a man you love. And Bhishma answers it. As long as he holds his bow, he says, no one can bring him down. But there is a warrior he will not fight. Shikhandi, Drupada's son, was born a daughter, and Bhishma has vowed never to raise a weapon against one he counts as a woman. Put Shikhandi in front, he tells them. Let Arjuna shoot from behind. Then the brothers walk back across the field, and the text lets us hear Arjuna come apart. He remembers being a small boy, climbing into Bhishma's lap, getting dust on his clothes, and calling him father. And Bhishma gently correcting him: not your father, child, your father's father. How can I kill him, Arjuna asks. Krishna steadies him. Arjuna has already promised to fight, and Bhishma himself has told them the way. Hold the scene for a moment. The enemy commander is also the family elder. He tells the truth even when the truth is his own death. And the grandson who must aim at him once sat in his lap. The text doesn't make any of it easy.
screen: `THE ENEMY WELCOMES THEM` · `"HOW CAN YOU BE DEFEATED?"` · `SHIKHANDI IN FRONT` · then, large: `A BOY IN HIS GRANDSIRE'S LAP`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your hands rest. Bring to mind one person whose counsel you would trust even when it's hard to hear. A teacher, an elder, an old friend. Breathing in, see their face. Breathing out, quietly name one question you would bring them, the way the brothers brought theirs across the field. You don't need their answer today. Just let the question be asked. If you pray, you can bring that question into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Bhishma's fall. Tonight it begins with a question asked in his own tent, and an honest answer that he gives against himself.
Your line: put Shikhandi in front. Today, if someone asks you a hard question, try giving the honest answer, even when it costs you a little. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

828.title: Bhishma's fall
828.hook: the warrior Bhishma won't fight carries a grievance from a whole lifetime before the war: the princess Amba
828.carry: a life that had nowhere to go
828.howItsDone: Amba's story is told in the Udyoga Parva of the Mahabharata, and retellings of the epic return to it when they reach Bhishma's fall, to explain why he will not fight Shikhandi.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was put Shikhandi in front, and the Pandavas went to his tent and asked him how. He told them: put Shikhandi in front. What honest answer did you give, or hold back? Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

Why Shikhandi? Bhishma has held off whole armies without flinching. Why would one warrior from Drupada's house make him lower his bow? The epic's answer starts long before this war, before the Pandavas were born, at a bride-choosing in the kingdom of Kashi. Bhishma arrives there, not for himself, but for his younger half-brother, who needs a wife. He carries off the princesses of Kashi in his chariot, and fights off the kings who chase him. One of those princesses is named Amba. Today, her story, because the arrow that brings Bhishma down was first aimed a lifetime ago.
screen: `WHY SHIKHANDI?` → `A BRIDE-CHOOSING IN KASHI.` → `A PRINCESS NAMED AMBA.`

segments.voice: Back in Hastinapura, Amba speaks up. Her heart, she says, was already given to King Shalva. Bhishma accepts that and lets her go to him. But Shalva won't take her back. Another man carried you off, he says in effect, go to him. And Bhishma won't take her back. He can't marry her himself: long ago he swore never to marry, the vow that, the text says, earned him the name Bhishma, the one of the terrible vow. Every door is shut, and in Amba's eyes one man shut them all. She looks for a champion. In the epic's telling, even Parashurama, Bhishma's own teacher, fights him on her behalf and can't defeat him. So Amba turns to austerity, and Shiva grants her wish: in another birth she will be the cause of Bhishma's death. She enters the fire. She is born again in the house of King Drupada, as a daughter, Shikhandini, raised as a son. Later, the text says, through an exchange with a yaksha, a nature spirit, she becomes a man, Shikhandi. And Bhishma knows all of it. When he refuses to fight Shikhandi, he's not only keeping a rule about fighting women. He's looking at Amba. The war's ending is braided out of an old wrong: a vow kept for a father, a princess carried off for a brother, a life that had nowhere to go. The epic never makes Bhishma a villain here. It lets his greatness and Amba's grievance both be true.
screen: `AMBA'S HEART BELONGS TO SHALVA` · `EVERY DOOR SHUT` · `SHIVA'S PROMISE` · then, large: `BORN AGAIN AS SHIKHANDI`

If you pray, you can name that person in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Bhishma's fall. It starts with a princess whose life had no open door, and a promise that she would be the cause of his death.
Your line: a life that had nowhere to go. Today, when someone is angry with you, ask quietly what older story they might be carrying. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

829.title: Bhishma's fall
829.hook: two kinds of arrows reach Bhishma, and he can tell them apart
829.howItsDone: The image of Bhishma on his bed of arrows, in Sanskrit shara-shayya, appears in temple art, paintings and retellings of the epic.

segments.voice: Your line was a life that had nowhere to go, and yesterday we went back a lifetime, to Amba, the princess who would be born again as Shikhandi. Whose older story did you notice? Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

Two kinds of arrows are flying at Bhishma's chariot. Some come from Shikhandi, standing in front, exactly as Bhishma himself advised. Bhishma doesn't answer them. He keeps his bow lowered toward that one warrior, the way he said he would. And behind Shikhandi, using him as cover, Arjuna is shooting too. Bhishma has trained and fought beside these archers for a lifetime. Today, the moment he stops guessing whose arrows are reaching him.

In Ganguli's English, Bhishma speaks as the arrows pierce him. These aren't Shikhandi's, he says, in effect. They cut too deep. These are Arjuna's. He names his grandson's arrows as they strike him, and he still doesn't turn his weapons on Shikhandi. Then he falls from his chariot. And here the epic gives a picture all its own. So many arrows are lodged in his body that he never touches the ground. He lies on them, held above the earth, on a bed of arrows. The fighting stops. Warriors on both sides drop their weapons and stand still. The Kauravas and the Pandavas, who were killing each other a moment ago, gather around the same old man. And Bhishma doesn't die. Long ago, the text says, his father granted him a gift for his vow: he would die only when he chose to. Lying there, he sees that the sun is moving in its southern course, and he decides it's not yet the time. He'll wait for the sun to turn north. The epic adds one more detail. Sages come to him in the form of swans, sent from his mother, the river goddess Ganga, and remind him of the sun's course, and he answers that he'll hold on. Bhishma's fall isn't a single crash. It's a man brought down by the truth he told, lying still on the field, choosing his own hour.
screen: `THESE ARE ARJUNA'S ARROWS` · `HE NEVER TOUCHES THE GROUND` · `BOTH ARMIES STAND STILL` · then, large: `HE CHOOSES HIS HOUR`

Breathe in, and let yourself be held. Breathe out, and let the noise around you go still, the way both armies went still around Bhishma. Nothing to fight for these two minutes. If you pray, you can rest in prayer, held. The bell holds the time.
Bhishma's fall. The grandsire on a bed of arrows, held above the ground, waiting for the sun to turn.
Your line: the bed of arrows. Today, when a fight around you stops for a moment, don't rush to restart it. Let the stillness stand. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

830.title: Bhishma's fall
830.hook: kings run up with soft pillows for the fallen grandsire, and he sends every one of them away
830.carry: a plea for peace that Duryodhana turned down
830.howItsDone: Some paintings and temple carvings show Bhishma on the bed of arrows with his head resting on Arjuna's arrows, and storytellers return to the pillow and the spring of water when they tell his fall.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhishma's fall itself: the arrows he knew as Arjuna's, the bed of arrows, both armies standing still. Did a moment of stillness come your way? Today, the last scene of this stretch. Day eight hundred thirty.

His body is held up by arrows, but his head isn't. It hangs down, unsupported. Bhishma asks for something to rest it on. And the kings around him do the obvious thing. They run to their tents and come back with pillows, soft ones, fine ones, the best in the camp. Bhishma looks at them and turns them all away. These don't belong on a bed like this one, he says, in effect. Then he looks at Arjuna. Today, what a grandson brings instead of a pillow, and the last thing Bhishma asks of the war.
screen: `HIS HEAD HANGS DOWN.` → `SOFT PILLOWS.` → `HE SENDS THEM AWAY.`

segments.voice: Bhishma asks Arjuna for a pillow fit for a hero's bed, and Arjuna understands. With tears in his eyes, the text says, he takes up his bow and drives arrows into the ground beneath Bhishma's head, so the head rests on them. A warrior's pillow for a warrior's bed. Bhishma is pleased. It's the same grandson whose arrows brought him down, and now his arrows are the only thing Bhishma will let hold him. Later Bhishma is thirsty. Again they bring the camp's best, cool water in fine vessels, and again he declines. He turns to Arjuna. And Arjuna shoots an arrow into the earth beside him, and a stream of pure, cool water springs up, and Bhishma drinks. Then the old man uses what strength he has left for one more piece of counsel, this time to Duryodhana. You've seen what Arjuna can do, he says, in Ganguli's telling. Let the war end with me. Make peace with your cousins, give them their share, and let everyone go home. Duryodhana hears it, and he doesn't take it. The war will go on. So that's Bhishma's fall: an honest answer in his own tent, an old wrong from Amba's life, arrows he recognized, a bed held above the earth, and a grandson who knew exactly what kind of pillow to bring. And one last plea for peace that nobody accepted.
screen: `A PILLOW OF ARROWS` · `WATER FROM THE EARTH` · `"LET THE WAR END WITH ME"` · then, large: `DURYODHANA REFUSES`

If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Bhishma's fall. It ends with a pillow of arrows, water drawn from the ground, and a plea for peace that went unheard.

831.title: Drona: Abhimanyu, Ghatotkacha, Drona's death
831.hook: Duryodhana asks his new commander for one thing: bring Yudhishthira to me alive
831.carry: the empty space where Arjuna should be
831.howItsDone: Drona is honored in Hindu tradition as the guru of the Kauravas and the Pandavas, and the Drona Parva, the book of the Mahabharata named for him, tells his command after Bhishma's fall.

segments.voice: Bhishma's fall ended with a pillow of arrows and a plea for peace that Duryodhana turned down. Did you ask anyone what they actually needed? Now the Kauravas need a new commander. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

A teacher takes command of an army sent against his own students. That's where the Kauravas are now. Bhishma lies on the field, and the man they choose to lead them is Drona, the master of arms who trained both sets of cousins as boys, who once tested the princes with a toy bird in a treetop and found that only Arjuna saw nothing but its head. Duryodhana honors him, and Drona, pleased, offers him a gift. Ask for whatever you want. Duryodhana's answer surprises him. Not Arjuna's death. Not victory. Bring me Yudhishthira, he says. Alive. Today, why he wanted him breathing.
screen: `THE TEACHER TAKES COMMAND.` → `ASK FOR ANYTHING.` → `"BRING ME YUDHISHTHIRA ALIVE."`

segments.voice: Drona is glad to hear it, at first. In Ganguli's telling, he praises Duryodhana: you don't want your cousin killed, so maybe you mean to make peace. But the text lets Duryodhana's reasons show. If Yudhishthira is captured, he can be drawn into the dice again, and the Pandavas can be sent back to the forest. Same game, second round. Drona agrees, with one condition he says out loud. He can take Yudhishthira only if Arjuna isn't standing beside him. Word of the promise reaches the Pandava camp, and Arjuna answers it plainly. While he lives, Drona won't lay a hand on his brother. So the Kauravas need Arjuna somewhere else. That's when a band of warriors from the Trigarta country steps forward and takes a dreadful oath. They'll challenge Arjuna, and they won't come back until they've killed him or died trying. They're called the samshaptakas, the sworn ones. And Arjuna won't refuse a challenge. He leaves another warrior to guard Yudhishthira, and rides away to fight them. Watch the pieces moving. A teacher's promise, a cousin's old game, an oath meant to draw one man off. In the coming days, that empty space where Arjuna should be will matter.
screen: `DRONA HOPES FOR PEACE` · `THE DICE AGAIN` · `ONLY IF ARJUNA IS AWAY` · then, large: `THE SWORN ONES`

If you pray, you can bring that request into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Drona. The teacher of the Kauravas and the Pandavas, now commanding the Kaurava army against his own students.

832.title: Drona: Abhimanyu, Ghatotkacha, Drona's death
832.hook: a young warrior knows how to break into the wheel formation, and says out loud that he doesn't know the way out
832.carry: one man at the gap undid it
832.howItsDone: Abhimanyu's entry into the chakravyuha is told in the Drona Parva of the Mahabharata and is retold in dance, theater and storytelling.

segments.voice: Yesterday Drona took command and promised to capture Yudhishthira, if only Arjuna were somewhere else. Your line: the empty space where Arjuna should be. Today, Arjuna is somewhere else. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

Morning, and across the field Drona has arranged his army into a shape the Pandavas dread: the chakra, the wheel. Ring inside ring of chariots, elephants and warriors, turning to close around anyone who comes near. On the Pandava side, only a few know how to break it. Arjuna knows. Krishna knows. And Arjuna is far away on the other side of the field, answering the sworn ones' challenge, just as the plan intended. Yudhishthira looks around and finds one more person who might know: Arjuna's son, Abhimanyu. Today, the conversation before he rides in.
screen: `THE WHEEL FORMATION.` → `ARJUNA IS FAR AWAY.` → `ARJUNA'S SON, ABHIMANYU.`

segments.voice: Abhimanyu is the son of Arjuna and Subhadra, Krishna's sister, young and fearless and already a fine warrior. Yudhishthira asks him to break the wheel. Abhimanyu's answer is honest in a way that's hard to read. In Ganguli's telling, he says he knows how to pierce the formation, but if trouble comes, he won't be able to come out again. Some retellings add a story that he learned the way in while still in his mother's womb, hearing it explained, and that she fell asleep before the way out. The epic passage here simply has him say what he knows and what he doesn't. Yudhishthira and Bhima reassure him. You break in, they say, and we'll follow right behind you, through the gap you make. So Abhimanyu drives in. He breaks the ring, and he's inside, fighting brilliantly. But behind him the gap doesn't stay open. Jayadratha, the king of Sindhu, rides into the breach. The text says he once won a gift from Shiva: for one day he could hold back all the Pandavas except Arjuna. This is that day. Bhima, Yudhishthira and the others hurl themselves at the opening and can't get through. The wheel closes. One young man is inside, alone, surrounded by Drona's army. The plan was sound, the courage was real, and one man at the gap undid it.
screen: `ARJUNA'S SON` · `"I KNOW THE WAY IN, NOT OUT"` · `"WE'LL FOLLOW YOU"` · then, large: `JAYADRATHA HOLDS THE GAP`

833.title: Drona: Abhimanyu, Ghatotkacha, Drona's death
833.hook: a young warrior with no bow, no horses and no sword picks up a chariot wheel
833.howItsDone: Abhimanyu's last stand inside the wheel formation is told in the Drona Parva and remembered in retellings, songs and stage plays, where he is honored for his courage.

segments.voice: Drona's wheel closed yesterday, with Abhimanyu inside and Jayadratha holding the gap. Your line was one man at the gap undid it. Today we stay inside the wheel with him. Day eight hundred thirty-three.

He has no bow anymore. His horses are down, his charioteer is gone, his sword is broken. And Abhimanyu bends down and picks up a chariot wheel, lifts it like a weapon, and keeps fighting. That picture is where the day ends up. It starts with him tearing through the Kaurava ranks inside the formation, so fiercely that, in Ganguli's telling, even Drona speaks admiringly of his skill. Today, the end of Abhimanyu, and the promise his father makes that night.
screen: `NO BOW, NO HORSES, NO SWORD.` → `HE LIFTS A CHARIOT WHEEL.` → `EVEN DRONA ADMIRES HIM.`

segments.voice: Admiration doesn't stop Drona from being a commander. In the text, he points out that while the boy holds his bow, he can't be beaten, so take the bow first. Karna cuts it from behind. Others bring down his horses and his charioteer. Then the great warriors of the Kaurava side close around one young man together, many against one. Abhimanyu fights on with sword and shield until those are broken, then with the chariot wheel, then with a mace. At last, the son of Duhshasana strikes him down with a mace, and Abhimanyu dies on the field. That evening, Arjuna rides back from his own fight and senses something is wrong before anyone says a word. When he learns what happened, and that Jayadratha held the gap, his grief turns into a vow. Before tomorrow's sun sets, he says, he'll kill Jayadratha. And if he fails, he'll enter the fire himself. Promises run all through these days: Drona's to Duryodhana, the sworn ones' oath, the uncles' word that they would follow. And now a father, back from the far side of the field, makes a vow with a sunset on it. The war keeps asking people what their promises are worth.
screen: `TAKE THE BOW FIRST` · `MANY AGAINST ONE` · `ABHIMANYU FALLS` · then, large: `ARJUNA'S VOW BEFORE SUNSET`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and if you'd like, rest one hand over your heart. Bring to mind someone young you care about, a child, a niece, a student, a younger friend. Breathe in, and picture them clearly. Breathe out, and wish them protection and a long road. If someone you loved died too young, let them be here as well, gently. If you pray, you can hold them all in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Drona. Today his army closes in on Abhimanyu, and Arjuna answers with a vow before sunset.
Your line: what their promises are worth. This week ends here. Today, look back at one promise you made this week, and see whether it's still yours to keep. Day eight hundred thirty-three.

match.prompt: Abhimanyu's last fight — tap the pairs.

myth: Abhimanyu was defeated in a fair one-on-one fight
many great warriors closed around him together.
Abhimanyu fought on with a chariot wheel
with his bow, horses and sword gone, he lifted a wheel and kept fighting.
Arjuna vowed to kill Jayadratha before the next sunset
and to enter the fire himself if he failed.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. you come back at evening and learn your son was killed while you were away, and Jayadratha held the gap. what do you do?
options: leave the war in grief.
vow to kill Jayadratha before the next sunset, or enter the fire.
demand that Drona hand over the warriors who surrounded him.
fork.reveal: Arjuna makes a vow with a deadline: Jayadratha by tomorrow's sunset, or the fire for himself.

original.note: the son of Arjuna and Subhadra, who broke into the wheel formation.

trapdoor: what you thought: Abhimanyu was just outnumbered.
what it means: he fell to many warriors at once, after his bow, horses and sword were taken from him.
what a scholar hears: Abhimanyu's death drives the next day's story: Arjuna's vow puts a sunset deadline on Jayadratha's life.
